title: Bloom filters: fast 'definitely not seen' checks

kcs.statement: A Bloom filter sets k hash positions in a bit array per inserted item. A lookup can return a false positive but never a false negative, so a 'no' answer is always correct.
For n items in m bits, the false positive rate is lowest when the number of hash functions is k = (m/n)·ln 2. About 10 bits per item gives roughly a 1% false positive rate.

problem_ideas: Implement add() and might_contain() over a Python int bitmask using k salted hashes, then test 10,000 inserts for false negatives.
Compute the bits needed for 1 billion URLs at a 1% false positive rate and convert it to gigabytes.
Given m = 8n, pick the k that minimises false positives and predict the rate.
A crawler uses a Bloom filter for seen URLs. Explain what a false positive costs: a page never gets crawled.
Explain why a plain Bloom filter cannot delete items and what a counting Bloom filter changes.
Place a Bloom filter in front of a disk-based key-value store to skip lookups for missing keys, and estimate the disk reads saved at a 90% miss rate.
